AI.conclusion: KAN-based pipeline successfully establishes analytical SoH degradation relationships from temperature data, offering interpretable, accurate modeling that bridges data-driven and analytical approaches for battery health management.

title: Distributed Safety-Critical Control of Multi-Agent Systems with Time-Varying Communication Topologies
summary: Coordinating multiple autonomous agents to reach a target region while avoiding collisions and maintaining communication connectivity is a core problem in multi-agent systems. In practice, agents have a limited communication range. Thus, network links appear and disappear as agents move, making the topology state-dependent and time-varying. Existing distributed solutions to multi-agent reach-avoid problems typically assume a fixed communication topology, and thus are not applicable when encountering discontinuities raised by time-varying topologies. This paper presents a distributed optimization-based control framework that addresses these challenges through two complementary mechanisms. First, we introduce a truncation function that converts the time-varying communication graph into a smoothly state-dependent one, ensuring that constraints remain continuous as communication links are created or removed. Second, we employ auxiliary mismatch variables with two-time-scale dynamics to decouple globally coupled state-dependent constraints, yielding a singular perturbation system that each agent can solve using only local information and neighbor communication. Through singular perturbation analysis, we prove that the distributed controller guarantees collision avoidance, connectivity preservation, and convergence to the target region. We validate the proposed framework through numerical simulations involving multi-agent navigation with obstacles and time-varying communication topologies.

AI.tldr: Distributed optimization-based control framework for multi-agent reach-avoid problems with time-varying communication topologies, using truncation functions and auxiliary mismatch variables to ensure collision avoidance, connectivity preservation, and target convergence.
AI.motivation: Existing distributed solutions for multi-agent reach-avoid problems typically assume fixed communication topologies, making them inapplicable when encountering discontinuities from time-varying topologies due to limited communication ranges in practical scenarios.
AI.method: Two complementary mechanisms: 1) truncation function that converts time-varying communication graph into smoothly state-dependent one, ensuring constraint continuity; 2) auxiliary mismatch variables with two-time-scale dynamics to decouple globally coupled state-dependent constraints, creating a singular perturbation system solvable by each agent using only local information and neighbor communication.
AI.result: Through singular perturbation analysis, the distributed controller guarantees collision avoidance, connectivity preservation, and convergence to the target region. Validated through numerical simulations involving multi-agent navigation with obstacles and time-varying communication topologies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses the challenges of time-varying communication topologies in multi-agent reach-avoid problems, providing a distributed solution that maintains safety and connectivity while achieving target convergence.

title: Incremental stability in $p=1$ and $p=\infty$: classification and synthesis
summary: All Lipschitz dynamics with the weak infinitesimal contraction (WIC) property can be expressed as a Lipschitz nonlinear system in proportional negative feedback -- this statement, a ``structure theorem,'' is true in the $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ norms. Equivalently, a Lipschitz vector field is WIC if and only if it can be written as a scalar decay plus a Lipschitz-bounded residual. We put this theorem to use using neural networks to approximate Lipschitz functions. This results in a map from unconstrained parameters to the set of WIC vector fields, enabling standard gradient-based training with no projections or penalty terms. Because the induced $1$- and $\infty$-norms of a matrix reduce to row or column sums, Lipschitz certification costs only $O(d^2)$ operations -- the same order as a forward pass and appreciably cheaper than eigenvalue or semidefinite methods for the $2$-norm. Numerical experiments on a planar flow-fitting task and a four-node opinion network demonstrate that the parameterization (re-)constructs contracting dynamics from trajectory data. In a discussion of the expressiveness of non-Euclidean contraction, we prove that the set of $2\times 2$ systems that contract in a weighted $1$- or $\infty$-norm is characterized by an eigenvalue cone, a strict subset of the Hurwitz region that quantifies the cost of moving away from the Euclidean norm.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a structure theorem showing that Lipschitz dynamics with weak infinitesimal contraction (WIC) can be expressed as Lipschitz nonlinear systems in proportional negative feedback in 1- and ∞-norms, enabling efficient neural network parameterization and training without projections or penalties.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical framework for learning contracting dynamical systems from data by establishing a theoretical foundation that enables efficient parameterization and training of WIC vector fields using neural networks, avoiding computationally expensive certification methods.
AI.method: Proves a structure theorem showing WIC vector fields can be expressed as scalar decay plus Lipschitz-bounded residual in 1- and ∞-norms. Uses neural networks to approximate Lipschitz functions, creating a map from unconstrained parameters to WIC vector fields. Leverages efficient Lipschitz certification (O(d²) operations) via induced matrix norms.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful reconstruction of contracting dynamics from trajectory data in planar flow-fitting and four-node opinion network experiments. Shows the parameterization enables standard gradient-based training without projections or penalty terms. Characterizes expressiveness of non-Euclidean contraction via eigenvalue cone analysis for 2×2 systems.
AI.conclusion: The structure theorem provides a practical framework for learning contracting dynamics, with efficient certification and training. The expressiveness analysis reveals that contraction in weighted 1- or ∞-norms corresponds to a strict subset of the Hurwitz region, quantifying the cost of moving away from Euclidean norms.

title: The QuadSoft: Design, Construction, and Experimental Validation of a Soft and Actuated Quadrotor
comment: Accepted for publication in the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2026)
summary: This paper presents QuadSoft, a novel fully actuated quadrotor equipped with continuous-curvature, tendon-driven soft robotic arms. The design combines a semi-rigid central frame with flexible arms, enabling controlled structural reconfiguration during flight without altering the propeller layout. Unlike existing soft aerial platforms that rely on discrete bending joints, QuadSoft utilizes a continuum deformation approach to modulate arm curvature, actively adjusting its thrust vector and aerodynamic characteristics. We characterize the geometric mapping between servomotor input and the resulting constant curvature, validating it experimentally. Outdoor flight tests demonstrate stable take-off, hover, directional maneuvers, and landing, confirming that controlled arm bending can generate horizontal displacement while preserving altitude. Measurements of pitch, roll, and curvature angles show that the platform follows intended actuation patterns with minimal attitude deviations. These results demonstrate that QuadSoft preserves the baseline stability of rigid quadrotors while enabling morphology-driven maneuverability, all under the standard PX4 autopilot without retuning. Beyond a proof of concept, this work establishes a distinctive outdoor validation of a tendon-driven continuum morphing quadrotor, opening a new research avenue toward adaptive aerial systems that combine the safety and versatility of soft robotics with the performance of conventional UAVs.

AI.tldr: QuadSoft is a novel fully actuated quadrotor with tendon-driven soft robotic arms that enables controlled structural reconfiguration during flight, allowing morphology-driven maneuverability while maintaining baseline stability under standard autopilot.
AI.motivation: To create an adaptive aerial system that combines the safety and versatility of soft robotics with the performance of conventional UAVs, addressing limitations of existing soft aerial platforms that rely on discrete bending joints rather than continuum deformation.
AI.method: Developed a fully actuated quadrotor with continuous-curvature, tendon-driven soft robotic arms combining semi-rigid central frame with flexible arms. Characterized geometric mapping between servomotor input and resulting constant curvature, validated experimentally. Used standard PX4 autopilot without retuning.
AI.result: Outdoor flight tests demonstrated stable take-off, hover, directional maneuvers, and landing. Controlled arm bending generated horizontal displacement while preserving altitude. Platform followed intended actuation patterns with minimal attitude deviations in pitch, roll, and curvature angles.
AI.conclusion: QuadSoft preserves baseline stability of rigid quadrotors while enabling morphology-driven maneuverability, establishing distinctive outdoor validation of tendon-driven continuum morphing quadrotors and opening new research avenues for adaptive aerial systems.

title: BLISS: Global Blind Identification of Linear Systems with Sparse Inputs
summary: Linear system identification and sparse dictionary learning can both be seen as structured matrix factorization problems. However, these two problems have historically been studied in isolation by the systems theory and machine learning communities. Although linear system identification enjoys a mature theory when inputs are known, blind linear system identification remains poorly understood beyond restrictive settings. In contrast, complete sparse dictionary learning has recently benefited from strong global identifiability results and scalable nonconvex algorithms. In this work, we bridge these two areas by showing that under a sparse input assumption, fully observed blind system identification becomes a generalization of complete dictionary learning. This connection allows us to develop global identifiability guarantees for blind system identification, by leveraging techniques from the complete dictionary learning literature. We further show empirically that a principled application of the alternating direction method of multipliers can globally recover the ground-truth system from a single trajectory, provided sufficient samples and input sparsity.

AI.tldr: Blind linear system identification with sparse inputs is connected to complete dictionary learning, enabling global identifiability guarantees and recovery via ADMM.
AI.motivation: Linear system identification and sparse dictionary learning are historically separate fields. While linear system identification has mature theory for known inputs, blind identification remains poorly understood. Meanwhile, complete sparse dictionary learning has strong identifiability results and algorithms.
AI.method: Bridge the two areas by showing blind system identification with sparse inputs generalizes complete dictionary learning. Leverage dictionary learning techniques for identifiability guarantees. Apply alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for recovery.
AI.result: Global identifiability guarantees for blind system identification derived from dictionary learning results. Empirical demonstration that ADMM can globally recover ground-truth system from single trajectory given sufficient samples and input sparsity.
AI.conclusion: Sparse input assumption connects blind system identification to dictionary learning, enabling theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms for previously challenging blind identification problems.

title: DeePC vs. Koopman MPC for Pasteurization: A Comparative Study
summary: Data-driven predictive control methods can provide the constraint handling and optimization of model predictive control (MPC) without first-principles models. Two such methods differ in how they replace the model: Data-enabled predictive control (DeePC) uses behavioral systems theory to predict directly from input--output trajectories via Hankel matrices, while Koopman-based MPC (KMPC) learns a lifted linear state-space representation from data. Both methods are well studied on their own, but head-to-head comparisons on multivariable process control problems are few. This paper compares them on a pasteurization unit with three manipulated inputs and three measured outputs, using a neural-network-based digital twin as the plant simulator. Both controllers share identical prediction horizons, cost weights, and constraints, so that differences in closed-loop behavior reflect the choice of predictive representation. Results show that both methods achieve feasible constrained control with comparable tracking error, but with a clear trade-off: KMPC tracks more tightly under the chosen cost, while DeePC produces substantially smoother input trajectories. These results help practitioners choose between the two approaches for thermal processing applications.

AI.tldr: Comparison of data-driven predictive control methods: DeePC uses behavioral systems theory with Hankel matrices, while KMPC learns lifted linear state-space representations via Koopman operators. Both achieve feasible constrained control on a pasteurization unit with comparable tracking, but KMPC tracks more tightly while DeePC produces smoother inputs.
AI.motivation: Data-driven predictive control methods offer constraint handling and optimization without first-principles models, but head-to-head comparisons of DeePC and KMPC on multivariable process control problems are limited. Understanding their relative performance helps practitioners choose appropriate methods for thermal processing applications.
AI.method: Comparative study using a pasteurization unit with three manipulated inputs and three measured outputs, employing a neural-network-based digital twin as plant simulator. Both controllers share identical prediction horizons, cost weights, and constraints to isolate differences in predictive representation. DeePC uses behavioral systems theory with Hankel matrices for direct prediction from input-output trajectories, while KMPC learns a lifted linear state-space representation from data via Koopman operators.
AI.result: Both methods achieve feasible constrained control with comparable tracking error. Clear trade-off observed: KMPC tracks more tightly under the chosen cost function, while DeePC produces substantially smoother input trajectories. Both approaches demonstrate effective constraint handling in the multivariable pasteurization control problem.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for choosing between DeePC and KMPC in thermal processing applications: KMPC offers tighter tracking performance, while DeePC provides smoother control actions. The results highlight that differences in closed-loop behavior reflect the choice of predictive representation rather than fundamental limitations of either approach.

title: Star-Tracker-Constrained Attitude MPC for CubeSats
summary: This paper presents an online linear model predictive control (MPC) framework for slew maneuvers that maintains star-tracker availability during ground-target tracking. The nonlinear rigid-body dynamics and geometric exclusion constraints are analytically linearized about the current state estimate at each control step, yielding a time-varying linear MPC formulation cast as a standard quadratic program (QP). This structure is compatible with established aerospace flight-software practices and offers a computational profile with lower online complexity than comparable nonlinear MPC schemes. The controller incorporates angular-rate, actuator, and star-tracker exclusion constraints over a receding horizon. Performance is assessed in high-fidelity nonlinear model-in-the-loop simulations using NASA's "42" spacecraft dynamics simulator, including a Monte Carlo campaign over varying target geometries and inertia perturbations.

AI.tldr: Online linear MPC for spacecraft slew maneuvers maintains star-tracker availability during ground-target tracking by analytically linearizing nonlinear dynamics and constraints at each control step.
AI.motivation: To enable spacecraft to perform slew maneuvers for ground-target tracking while maintaining star-tracker availability, which is typically lost during such maneuvers due to geometric exclusion constraints.
AI.method: Analytically linearizes nonlinear rigid-body dynamics and geometric exclusion constraints about current state estimates at each control step, creating time-varying linear MPC formulated as quadratic program (QP). Incorporates angular-rate, actuator, and star-tracker exclusion constraints over receding horizon.
AI.result: Controller achieves lower online computational complexity than comparable nonlinear MPC schemes while maintaining compatibility with aerospace flight-software practices. Performance validated through high-fidelity nonlinear model-in-the-loop simulations using NASA's "42" spacecraft dynamics simulator with Monte Carlo campaign.
AI.conclusion: The proposed online linear MPC framework successfully enables spacecraft to perform ground-target tracking maneuvers while maintaining star-tracker availability, offering computational efficiency and practical implementation advantages over nonlinear MPC approaches.

title: Beyond Bounded Noise: Stochastic Set-Membership Estimation for Nonlinear Systems
summary: In this paper, we derive a novel procedure for set-membership estimation of dynamical systems affected by stochastic noise with unbounded support. By employing a bound on the sample covariance matrix, we are able to provide a finite-sample uncertainty set containing the true system parameters with high probability. Our approach can be natively applied to a wide class of nonlinear systems affected by sub- Gaussian noise. Through our analysis, we provide conditions under which the proposed uncertainty set converges to the true system parameters and establish an upper bound on the convergence rate. The proposed uncertainty set can be used directly for the synthesis of robust controllers with probabilistic stability and performance guarantees. Concluding numerical examples demonstrate the advantages of the proposed formulation over established approaches.

AI.tldr: Novel finite-sample set-membership estimation for dynamical systems with unbounded stochastic noise using covariance bounds to create high-probability uncertainty sets for robust control synthesis.
AI.motivation: Existing set-membership estimation methods typically assume bounded noise, but many real-world systems experience stochastic noise with unbounded support (e.g., Gaussian noise). There's a need for finite-sample guarantees for parameter estimation in such systems to enable robust controller synthesis with probabilistic stability guarantees.
AI.method: Derives a novel procedure using bounds on the sample covariance matrix to construct finite-sample uncertainty sets containing true system parameters with high probability. The approach applies natively to a wide class of nonlinear systems affected by sub-Gaussian noise, providing conditions for convergence and establishing upper bounds on convergence rates.
AI.result: The method provides finite-sample uncertainty sets with high-probability guarantees, conditions under which these sets converge to true parameters, and explicit convergence rate bounds. Numerical examples demonstrate advantages over established approaches, and the uncertainty sets can be directly used for robust controller synthesis with probabilistic stability and performance guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The proposed set-membership estimation framework successfully handles dynamical systems with unbounded stochastic noise, providing finite-sample guarantees and enabling robust control synthesis with probabilistic stability assurances, outperforming existing methods in numerical validation.

title: Robust IMMPC: An Offset-free MPC for Rejecting Unknown Disturbances
summary: Output regulation is the problem of finding a control input to asymptotically track reference trajectories and reject disturbances. This can be addressed by using the internal model principle to embed a model of the disturbance in the controller. In this work, we present a Model Predictive Control scheme to achieve offset-free control. To do so, we extend Internal Model MPC to general bounded disturbances that must not be generated by the disturbance model. We show recursive feasibility, constraint satisfaction, and provide convergence conditions for the optimal reachable output. The proposed controller is validated on a four-tank system.

AI.tldr: Model Predictive Control scheme for offset-free regulation using Internal Model Principle extended to general bounded disturbances, with guarantees for recursive feasibility, constraint satisfaction, and convergence to optimal reachable output.
AI.motivation: Address the output regulation problem for asymptotic tracking and disturbance rejection, particularly extending Internal Model MPC to handle general bounded disturbances that are not necessarily generated by the disturbance model.
AI.method: Extends Internal Model MPC to accommodate general bounded disturbances, incorporates disturbance model in controller design using Internal Model Principle, and develops Model Predictive Control scheme with guarantees for offset-free control.
AI.result: Proves recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction, provides convergence conditions for optimal reachable output, and validates controller performance on a four-tank system.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPC scheme successfully achieves offset-free control for general bounded disturbances with theoretical guarantees and practical validation on a benchmark system.

title: Typical Scenarios Generation Method Considering System-level Characteristics of Power System
summary: This paper proposes a method for generating typical scenarios based on system-level macroscopic characteristics of power system and considering its stability properties. First, considering uncertainties such as renewable energy generation in power-electronics-dominated power systems, multidimensional scaling is used to construct an electrical coordinate system. Based on this, system-level characteristics of the distribution of physical quantities, such as power generation and load, are characterized. Furthermore, a method for generating typical scenarios based on the system's system-level characteristics and stability properties is proposed. For the obtained joint probability distribution of system-level characteristics, weighted Mahalanobis distance can be used to predict the stability properties of random scenarios. Finally, the typicality and representativeness of the scenarios generated by the proposed method with respect to stability properties are verified on the CSEE benchmark case, and stability prediction for random scenarios is achieved using a probabilistic testing method.

AI.tldr: A method for generating typical power system scenarios based on system-level macroscopic characteristics and stability properties, using multidimensional scaling and weighted Mahalanobis distance for stability prediction.
AI.motivation: To address uncertainties in renewable energy generation in power-electronics-dominated power systems and develop a systematic approach for generating representative scenarios that capture both system-level characteristics and stability properties.
AI.method: 1. Use multidimensional scaling to construct an electrical coordinate system considering uncertainties like renewable energy generation. 2. Characterize system-level distribution of physical quantities (power generation, load). 3. Generate typical scenarios based on system-level characteristics and stability properties. 4. Use weighted Mahalanobis distance to predict stability properties from joint probability distribution of system-level characteristics.
AI.result: The method successfully generates typical scenarios with verified typicality and representativeness regarding stability properties on the CSEE benchmark case. Stability prediction for random scenarios is achieved using a probabilistic testing method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively generates representative power system scenarios that incorporate both macroscopic characteristics and stability considerations, enabling reliable stability prediction for random scenarios through probabilistic testing.

title: Toward Efficient Deployment and Synchronization in Digital Twins-Empowered Networks
summary: Digital twins (DTs) are envisioned as a key enabler of the cyber-physical continuum in future wireless networks. However, efficient deployment and synchronization of DTs in dynamic multi-access edge computing (MEC) environments remains challenging due to time-varying communication and computational resources. This paper investigates the joint optimization of DT deployment and synchronization in dynamic MEC environments. A deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework is proposed for adaptive DT placement and association to minimize interaction latency between physical and digital entities. To ensure semantic freshness, an update scheduling policy is further designed to minimize the long-term weighted sum of the Age of Changed Information (AoCI) and the update cost. A relative policy iteration algorithm with a threshold-based structure is developed to derive the optimal policy. Simulation results show that the proposed methods achieve lower latency, enhanced information freshness, and reduced system cost compared with benchmark schemes

AI.tldr: DRL-based framework for optimizing digital twin deployment and synchronization in dynamic MEC environments to minimize latency and maintain information freshness
AI.motivation: Digital twins are crucial for cyber-physical continuum in future wireless networks, but efficient deployment and synchronization in dynamic MEC environments is challenging due to time-varying communication and computational resources
AI.method: Deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive DT placement and association, plus update scheduling policy with relative policy iteration algorithm with threshold-based structure to minimize AoCI and update cost
AI.result: Simulation results show lower latency, enhanced information freshness, and reduced system cost compared to benchmark schemes
AI.conclusion: Proposed DRL framework effectively optimizes DT deployment and synchronization in dynamic MEC environments, achieving superior performance in latency, freshness, and cost metrics

title: Optimal GNSS Time Tracking for Long-term Stable Time Realisation in Synchronised Atomic Clocks
summary: In this manuscript, we propose a novel optimal Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) time tracking algorithm to collectively steer an ensemble consisting of synchronising miniature atomic clocks towards standard GNSS time. The synchronising miniature atomic clocks generate a common synchronised time which has good short term performance but its accuracy and precision, which is measured by Allan variance, deteriorates in the long run. So, a supervisor designs and periodically broadcasts the proposed GNSS time tracking control to the ensemble miniature atomic clocks that steer the average of ensemble towards the average of GNSS receivers, which are receivers of GNSS time. The tracking control is constructed using a Kalman filter estimation process that estimates the difference in average of GNSS receivers and average of ensemble clocks by using relative clock readings between GNSS receivers and their adjacent ensemble clock. Under the influence of the periodically received tracking control, the stabilised ensemble clocks have better long term accuracy and precision over long averaging periods. Since the tracking control is designed to solely influence the average of the ensemble, the tracking process does not interfere with the synchronisation process and vice versa. The feedback matrix associated with the tracking control is obtained from an optimisation problem that minimises steady-state Allan variance. Numerical results are provided to show the efficacy of the proposed algorithm for enhancing long term performance.

AI.tldr: A novel optimal GNSS time tracking algorithm that steers an ensemble of synchronizing miniature atomic clocks toward standard GNSS time using Kalman filter-based control to improve long-term accuracy and precision without interfering with short-term synchronization.
AI.motivation: Miniature atomic clocks in ensembles provide good short-term synchronized time but suffer from deteriorating accuracy and precision (measured by Allan variance) over long periods, requiring a solution to maintain long-term performance while preserving short-term synchronization.
AI.method: A supervisor periodically broadcasts GNSS time tracking control to the ensemble using a Kalman filter that estimates the difference between GNSS receiver averages and ensemble clock averages based on relative clock readings. The feedback matrix is optimized to minimize steady-state Allan variance, ensuring the control only affects ensemble averages without disrupting synchronization.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm stabilizes ensemble clocks with improved long-term accuracy and precision over extended averaging periods, as demonstrated through numerical results showing enhanced long-term performance.
AI.conclusion: The optimal GNSS time tracking algorithm successfully enhances long-term performance of synchronized miniature atomic clock ensembles while maintaining their short-term synchronization capabilities, providing an effective solution for applications requiring both short-term precision and long-term accuracy.

title: Battery Electric Truck Infrastructure Co-design via Joint Optimization and Agent-based Simulation
summary: As zero-emission zones emerge in European cities, fleet operators are shifting to electric vehicles. To maintain their current operations, a clear understanding of the charging infrastructure required and its relationship to existing power grid limitations is needed. This study presents an optimization frame-work for jointly designing charging infrastructure and schedules within a logistics distribution network, validated through agent-based simulations. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer linear program and develop an agent-based model to evaluate various designs and operations under stochastic conditions. Our experiments compare rule-based and optimized strategies in a case study of the Netherlands. Results show that current commercial solutions suffice for middle-mile logistics, with central co-design yielding average cost reductions of 5.2% to 6.4% and an average 20.1% decrease in total installed power. While rule-based control effectively manages charging operations and mitigates delays, optimizing charge scheduling significantly reduces queuing times (99%), charging costs (13.5%), and time spent near capacity (10.9%). Our optimization-simulation framework paves the way for combining optimized infrastructure planning and realistic fleet operations in digital-twin environments.

AI.tldr: Optimization framework for joint design of EV charging infrastructure and schedules in logistics networks, showing significant cost and efficiency improvements through central co-design.
AI.motivation: European cities implementing zero-emission zones require fleet operators to transition to electric vehicles, necessitating understanding of charging infrastructure requirements and power grid limitations for maintaining current operations.
AI.method: Mixed-integer linear programming formulation for optimization combined with agent-based simulations to evaluate designs under stochastic conditions; validated through case study in the Netherlands comparing rule-based and optimized strategies.
AI.result: Current commercial solutions suffice for middle-mile logistics; central co-design yields 5.2-6.4% cost reductions and 20.1% decrease in installed power; optimized scheduling reduces queuing times by 99%, charging costs by 13.5%, and time spent near capacity by 10.9%.
AI.conclusion: The optimization-simulation framework enables combining optimized infrastructure planning with realistic fleet operations in digital-twin environments, providing practical solutions for EV logistics transition.

title: Explicit MPC for Parameter Dependent Linear Systems
summary: This paper presents two explicit Model Predictive Control formulations for linear systems parameterized in terms of design variables. Such parameter dependent behavior commonly arises from operating point dependent linearization of nonlinear systems as well as from variations in mechanical, electrical, or thermal properties associated with material selection in the design of the process or system components. In contrast to explicit MPC approaches that treat design parameter variations and dependencies as disturbances, the proposed methods incorporate the parameters directly into the system matrices in an affine manner. However, explicitly incorporating these dependencies significantly increases the complexity of explicit MPC formulations due to resulting nonlinear terms involving decision variables and parameters. We address this complexity by proposing two approximation methods. Both methods are applied to two examples, and their performances are compared with respect to the exact eMPC implementation.

AI.tldr: Two explicit MPC formulations for linear systems with design parameters, using approximations to handle complexity from parameter dependencies.
AI.motivation: Parameter-dependent linear systems arise from nonlinear system linearization at different operating points and material property variations in system design. Existing explicit MPC approaches treat parameters as disturbances rather than incorporating them directly into system matrices.
AI.method: Two approximation methods for explicit MPC that incorporate design parameters directly into system matrices in an affine manner, addressing complexity from nonlinear terms involving decision variables and parameters.
AI.result: Both methods are applied to two examples and their performances are compared against exact explicit MPC implementation.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents practical approaches for handling parameter dependencies in explicit MPC through approximation methods that reduce computational complexity while maintaining performance.

title: Analytical Probabilistic Power Flow Approximation Using Invertible Neural Networks
summary: Probabilistic power flow (PPF) is essential for quantifying operational uncertainty in modern distribution systems with high penetration of renewable generation and flexible loads. Conventional PPF methods primarily rely on Monte Carlo (MC) based power flow (PF) simulations or simplified analytical approximations. While MC approaches are computationally intensive and demand substantial data storage, analytical approximations often compromise accuracy. In this paper, we propose a novel analytical PPF framework that eliminates the dependence on MC-based PF simulations and, in principle, enables an approximation of the analytical form of arbitrary voltage distributions. The core idea is to learn an explicit and invertible mapping between stochastic power injections and system voltages using invertible neural networks (INNs). By leveraging the Change of Variable Theorem, the proposed framework facilitates direct approximation of the analytical form of voltage probability distributions without repeated PF computations. Extensive numerical studies demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance both as a high-accuracy PF solver and as an efficient analytical PPF estimator.

AI.tldr: Proposes an analytical PPF framework using invertible neural networks to directly approximate voltage distributions without Monte Carlo simulations, achieving high accuracy as both PF solver and PPF estimator.
AI.motivation: Conventional PPF methods face limitations: Monte Carlo approaches are computationally intensive and require substantial data storage, while analytical approximations often sacrifice accuracy. There's a need for efficient yet accurate PPF methods for modern distribution systems with high renewable penetration.
AI.method: Uses invertible neural networks (INNs) to learn an explicit and invertible mapping between stochastic power injections and system voltages. Leverages the Change of Variable Theorem to directly approximate the analytical form of voltage probability distributions without repeated power flow computations.
AI.result: Extensive numerical studies demonstrate state-of-the-art performance: the framework achieves high accuracy as both a power flow solver and an efficient analytical PPF estimator, eliminating dependence on Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed INN-based analytical PPF framework provides an efficient and accurate alternative to conventional methods, enabling direct approximation of voltage distributions without computational burdens of Monte Carlo simulations while maintaining analytical rigor.

title: Neural Vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin Certificates for Delayed Interconnected Systems
summary: Ensuring scalable input-to-state stability (sISS) is critical for the safety and reliability of large-scale interconnected systems, especially in the presence of communication delays. While learning-based controllers can achieve strong empirical performance, their black-box nature makes it difficult to provide formal and scalable stability guarantees. To address this gap, we propose a framework to synthesize and verify neural vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin certificates for discrete-time delayed interconnected systems. Our contributions are three-fold. First, we establish a sufficient condition for discrete-time sISS via vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin functions, which enables certification for large-scale delayed interconnected systems. Second, we develop a scalable synthesis and verification framework that learns the neural certificates and verifies the certificates on reachability-constrained delay domains with scalability analysis. Third, we validate our approach on mixed-autonomy platoons, drone formations, and microgrids against multiple baselines, showing improved verification efficiency with competitive control performance.

AI.tldr: A framework for synthesizing and verifying neural vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin certificates to ensure scalable input-to-state stability for discrete-time delayed interconnected systems.
AI.motivation: Learning-based controllers offer strong empirical performance but lack formal stability guarantees due to their black-box nature, especially for large-scale interconnected systems with communication delays where scalable input-to-state stability (sISS) is critical for safety and reliability.
AI.method: Proposes a framework with three key components: 1) establishes sufficient condition for discrete-time sISS via vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin functions, 2) develops scalable synthesis and verification framework that learns neural certificates and verifies them on reachability-constrained delay domains, 3) includes scalability analysis.
AI.result: Validated on mixed-autonomy platoons, drone formations, and microgrids against multiple baselines, showing improved verification efficiency with competitive control performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully bridges the gap between learning-based controllers' empirical performance and formal stability guarantees for large-scale delayed interconnected systems, providing both scalable synthesis and verification of neural certificates.

title: Min-Max Grassmannian Optimization for Online Subspace Tracking
comment: Submitted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, December 15-18 2026, Honolulu, Hawaii, USA
summary: This paper discusses robustness guarantees for online tracking of time-varying subspaces from noisy data. Building on recent work in optimization over a Grassmannian manifold, we introduce a new approach for robust subspace tracking by modeling data uncertainty in a Grassmannian ball. The robust subspace tracking problem is cast into a min-max optimization framework, for which we derive a closed-form solution for the worst-case subspace, enabling a geometric robustness adjustment that is both analytically tractable and computationally efficient, unlike iterative convex relaxations. The resulting algorithm, GeRoST (Geometrically Robust Subspace Tracking), is validated on two case studies: tracking a linear time-varying system and online foreground-background separation in video.

AI.tldr: GeRoST: A geometrically robust subspace tracking algorithm using min-max optimization over Grassmannian manifolds with closed-form worst-case solutions for time-varying subspace estimation from noisy data.
AI.motivation: Need for robust online tracking of time-varying subspaces from noisy data, addressing limitations of existing methods that lack analytical tractability or computational efficiency.
AI.method: Models data uncertainty in a Grassmannian ball, formulates robust subspace tracking as min-max optimization over Grassmannian manifold, derives closed-form solution for worst-case subspace enabling geometric robustness adjustment.
AI.result: Developed GeRoST algorithm that is both analytically tractable and computationally efficient, validated on tracking linear time-varying systems and online foreground-background separation in video.
AI.conclusion: GeRoST provides a novel geometrically robust approach to subspace tracking with closed-form solutions that outperforms iterative convex relaxations in terms of analytical tractability and computational efficiency.

title: Bridging RL and MPC for mixed-integer optimal control with application to Formula 1 race strategies
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures; This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: We propose a hybrid reinforcement learning (RL) and model predictive control (MPC) framework for mixed-integer optimal control, where discrete variables enter the cost and dynamics but not the constraints. Existing hierarchical approaches use RL only for the discrete action space, leaving continuous optimization to MPC. Unlike these methods, we train the RL agent on the full hybrid action space, ensuring consistency with the cost of the underlying Markov decision process. During deployment, the RL actor is rolled out over the prediction horizon to parametrize an integer-free nonlinear MPC through the discrete action sequence and provide a continuous warm-start. The learned critic serves as a terminal cost to capture long-term performance. We prove recursive feasibility, and validate the framework on a Formula 1 race strategy problem. The hybrid method achieves near-optimal performance relative to an offline mixed-integer nonlinear program benchmark, outperforming a standalone RL agent. Moreover, the hybrid scheme enables adaptation to unseen disturbances through modular MPC extensions at zero retraining cost.

AI.tldr: Hybrid RL-MPC framework for mixed-integer optimal control that trains RL on full hybrid action space, uses RL actor to parametrize integer-free MPC during deployment, and employs critic as terminal cost for long-term performance.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical approaches for mixed-integer optimal control use RL only for discrete action space while leaving continuous optimization to MPC, which may not ensure consistency with the underlying Markov decision process cost structure.
AI.method: Train RL agent on full hybrid (discrete+continuous) action space; during deployment, roll out RL actor over prediction horizon to parametrize integer-free nonlinear MPC through discrete action sequence and provide continuous warm-start; use learned critic as terminal cost for long-term performance.
AI.result: Proves recursive feasibility; achieves near-optimal performance relative to offline mixed-integer nonlinear program benchmark on Formula 1 race strategy problem; outperforms standalone RL agent; enables adaptation to unseen disturbances through modular MPC extensions without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid RL-MPC framework effectively combines the strengths of both approaches for mixed-integer optimal control problems, providing near-optimal performance, theoretical guarantees, and practical adaptability to disturbances without additional training.

title: Soft projections for robust data-driven control
summary: We consider data-based predictive control based on behavioral systems theory. In the linear setting this means that a system is described as a subspace of trajectories, and predictive control can be formulated using a projection onto the intersection of this behavior and a constraint set. Instead of learning the model, or subspace, we focus on determining this projection from data. Motivated by the use of regularization in data-enabled predictive control (DeePC), we introduce the use of soft projections, which approximate the true projector onto the behavior from noisy data. In the simplest case, these are equivalent to known regularized DeePC schemes, but they exhibit a number of benefits. First, we provide a bound on the approximation error consisting of a bias and a variance term that can be traded-off by the regularization weight. The derived bound is independent of the true system order, highlighting the benefit of soft projections compared to low-dimensional subspace estimates. Moreover, soft projections allow for intuitive generalizations, one of which we show has superior performance on a case study. Finally, we provide update formulas for soft projectors enabling the efficient adaptation of the proposed data-driven control methods in the case of streaming data.

AI.tldr: Soft projections for data-driven predictive control provide regularization benefits with error bounds independent of system order, enabling efficient adaptation to streaming data.
AI.motivation: Motivated by regularization in DeePC, the paper addresses the challenge of determining projections onto system behaviors from noisy data without explicit model learning, aiming to improve data-driven control performance.
AI.method: Introduces soft projections that approximate true projectors onto system behaviors from noisy data, providing regularization with tunable weights that trade off bias and variance, and includes update formulas for streaming data adaptation.
AI.result: Derives error bounds independent of true system order, shows equivalence to known regularized DeePC schemes in simplest cases, demonstrates superior performance in case studies, and provides efficient update mechanisms for streaming data.
AI.conclusion: Soft projections offer a flexible framework for data-driven predictive control with regularization benefits, system-order-independent error bounds, intuitive generalizations, and efficient adaptation to streaming data scenarios.

title: Dispatch-Embedded Long-Term Tail Risk Assessment and Mitigation via CVaR for Renewable Power Systems
summary: Renewable energy (RE) generation exhibits pronounced seasonality and variability, and neglecting these features can lead to significant underestimation of long-term power system risks in power supply. While long-term dispatch strategies are essential for evaluating and mitigating tail risks, they are often excluded from existing models due to their complexity. This paper proposes a long-term tail risk assessment and mitigation framework for renewable power systems, explicitly embedding dispatch strategies. A representative scenario generation method is designed, combining multi-timescale Copula modeling to capture RE's long-range variability and correlation. Building on these scenarios, an evolution-based risk assessment model is established, where Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) is employed as a robust metric to quantify tail risks. Finally, a controlled evolution-based risk mitigation scheme is introduced to refine long-term dispatch strategies for mitigating tail risks. Case studies on a modified IEEE-39 bus system incorporating real-world data substantiate the efficacy of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A framework for assessing and mitigating long-term tail risks in renewable power systems by embedding dispatch strategies, using multi-timescale Copula modeling for scenario generation and CVaR for risk quantification.
AI.motivation: Renewable energy's seasonality and variability are often neglected in existing models, leading to underestimation of long-term power system risks. Long-term dispatch strategies are crucial for evaluating tail risks but are typically excluded due to complexity.
AI.method: Proposes a three-part framework: 1) Representative scenario generation using multi-timescale Copula modeling to capture RE's long-range variability and correlation; 2) Evolution-based risk assessment model using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to quantify tail risks; 3) Controlled evolution-based risk mitigation scheme to refine long-term dispatch strategies.
AI.result: Case studies on a modified IEEE-39 bus system with real-world data demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in assessing and mitigating long-term tail risks in renewable power systems.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully addresses the gap in existing models by explicitly embedding long-term dispatch strategies for tail risk assessment and mitigation in renewable power systems, providing a robust approach to manage seasonal and variable renewable generation.

title: Mean-Field Control of Adherence in Participation-Coupled Vehicle Rebalancing Systems
summary: Human driver participation is a critical source of uncertainty in Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) rebalancing. Drivers follow platform recommendations probabilistically, and their willingness to comply evolves with experienced outcomes. This creates a closed-loop feedback in which stronger recommendations increase participation, participation increases congestion, congestion lowers allocation success, and realized allocations update adherence beliefs. We propose a microscopic stochastic model that couples (i) belief-driven participation, (ii) Poisson demand, (iii) uniform matching, and (iv) Beta--Bernoulli belief updates. Under a large-population closure, we derive a deterministic mean-field recursion for the population adherence state under platform actuation. For i.i.d. Poisson demand and constant recommendation intensity, we prove global well-posedness and invariance of the recursion, establish equilibrium existence, provide uniqueness conditions, and show global convergence in the regime where platform recommendations are no weaker than baseline participation. We then define steady-state adherence and throughput, characterize the induced performance frontier, and show that adherence and throughput cannot, in general, be simultaneously maximized under uniform time-invariant actuation. This yields a throughput-maximization problem with an adherence floor. Exploiting the monotone frontier structure, we show the optimal uniform time-invariant policy is the maximal feasible recommendation intensity and provide an efficient bisection-based algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a stochastic model for Mobility-on-Demand rebalancing with belief-driven driver participation, analyzes equilibrium behavior, and solves for optimal recommendation policies under adherence constraints.
AI.motivation: Human driver participation uncertainty in MoD systems creates closed-loop feedback where recommendations affect participation, which affects congestion and allocation success, which in turn updates driver beliefs about compliance. This complex feedback loop needs mathematical modeling to understand system behavior and optimize platform recommendations.
AI.method: Proposes a microscopic stochastic model coupling belief-driven participation, Poisson demand, uniform matching, and Beta-Bernoulli belief updates. Derives deterministic mean-field recursion under large-population closure. Analyzes equilibrium properties, establishes global convergence conditions, and formulates throughput-maximization with adherence constraints.
AI.result: Proves global well-posedness and invariance of the mean-field recursion, establishes equilibrium existence, provides uniqueness conditions, shows global convergence when recommendations are no weaker than baseline participation. Characterizes performance frontier showing trade-off between adherence and throughput, and develops efficient bisection algorithm for optimal uniform time-invariant policy.
AI.conclusion: Adherence and throughput cannot be simultaneously maximized under uniform time-invariant actuation, creating a fundamental trade-off. The optimal policy is the maximal feasible recommendation intensity that meets adherence constraints, and the monotone frontier structure enables efficient computation via bisection.

title: Tube-Based Safety for Anticipative Tracking in Multi-Agent Systems
comment: This work has been submitted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control for possible publication
summary: A tube-based safety framework is presented for robust anticipative tracking in nonlinear Brunovsky multi-agent systems subject to bounded disturbances. The architecture establishes robust safety certificates for a feedforward-augmented ancillary control policy. By rendering the state-deviation dynamics independent of the agents' internal nonlinearities, the formulation strictly circumvents the restrictive Lipschitz-bound feasibility conditions otherwise required for robust stabilization. Consequently, this structure admits an explicit, closed-form robust positively invariant (RPI) tube radius that systematically attenuates the exponential control barrier function (eCBF) tightening margins, thereby mitigating constraint conservatism while preserving formal forward invariance. Within the distributed model predictive control (MPC) layer, mapping the local tube radii through the communication graph yields a closed-form global formation error bound formulated via the minimum singular value of the augmented Laplacian. Robust inter-agent safety is enforced with minimal communication overhead, requiring only a single scalar broadcast per neighbor at initialization. Numerical simulations confirm the framework's efficacy in safely navigating heterogeneous formations through cluttered environments.

AI.tldr: Tube-based safety framework for robust anticipative tracking in nonlinear multi-agent systems with bounded disturbances, enabling closed-form robust invariant tubes and distributed safety enforcement with minimal communication.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of robust safety certification for nonlinear multi-agent systems subject to disturbances while avoiding restrictive Lipschitz-bound feasibility conditions typically required for robust stabilization.
AI.method: Feedforward-augmented ancillary control policy that renders state-deviation dynamics independent of agents' internal nonlinearities, enabling explicit closed-form robust positively invariant (RPI) tube radius computation. Uses exponential control barrier function (eCBF) tightening with systematic attenuation, and distributed MPC with tube radii mapping through communication graph.
AI.result: Framework establishes robust safety certificates, circumvents Lipschitz-bound feasibility conditions, provides closed-form global formation error bound via minimum singular value of augmented Laplacian, and enforces robust inter-agent safety with minimal communication (single scalar broadcast per neighbor at initialization).
AI.conclusion: The tube-based safety framework successfully enables robust anticipative tracking in nonlinear multi-agent systems with bounded disturbances, mitigating constraint conservatism while preserving formal forward invariance, with numerical simulations confirming efficacy in safely navigating heterogeneous formations through cluttered environments.

title: A Functional Learning Approach for Team-Optimal Traffic Coordination
summary: In this paper, we develop a kernel-based policy iteration functional learning framework for computing team-optimal strategies in traffic coordination problems. We consider a multi-agent discrete-time linear system with a cost function that combines quadratic regulation terms and nonlinear safety penalties. Building on the Hilbert space formulation of offline receding-horizon policy iteration, we seek approximate solutions within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where the policy improvement step is implemented via a discrete Fréchet derivative. We further study the model-free receding-horizon scenario, where the system dynamics are estimated using recursive least squares, followed by updating the policy using rolling online data. The proposed method is tested in signal-free intersection scenarios via both model-based and model-free simulations and validated in SUMO.

AI.tldr: Kernel-based policy iteration framework for team-optimal traffic coordination in multi-agent systems with safety constraints, tested in signal-free intersections.
AI.motivation: Need for effective traffic coordination strategies in multi-agent systems, particularly for signal-free intersections, requiring methods that handle both optimal control objectives and safety constraints.
AI.method: Kernel-based policy iteration functional learning framework using reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, with discrete Fréchet derivative for policy improvement. Two approaches: model-based offline receding-horizon and model-free online with recursive least squares estimation.
AI.result: Method tested in signal-free intersection scenarios via both model-based and model-free simulations, with validation in SUMO traffic simulation software.
AI.conclusion: Proposed kernel-based policy iteration framework provides effective approach for computing team-optimal strategies in traffic coordination problems with safety constraints, applicable to both model-based and model-free scenarios.

title: Maximizing Power Flexibility of Hybrid Energy Systems for Capacity Market
summary: Hybrid Energy Systems (HES), integrating generation sources, energy storage, and controllable loads, are well-positioned to provide real-time grid flexibility. However, quantifying this maximum flexibility is challenging due to renewable generation uncertainty and the complexity of power allocation across multiple assets in real time. This paper presents a rule-based framework for characterizing HES flexibility and systematically allocating power among its constituent assets. The flexibility envelope defines the dynamic power boundary within which the HES can inject or absorb power without violating operational constraints. Shaped in real time by capacity bids, available solar generation, and power allocation protocol, it enables reliable and predictable HES participation in regulation markets. Depending on the operational objective, the framework supports both symmetric and asymmetric flexibility cases. Further, the proposed power-allocation rule is benchmarked against an optimal dispatch, providing a performance reference under realistic conditions. Finally, state of charge drift correction control is presented to ensure sustained battery operation and system reliability. This work, therefore, offers a rigorous and practical framework for integrating HES into capacity markets through effective flexibility characterization.

AI.tldr: A rule-based framework for characterizing Hybrid Energy Systems (HES) flexibility and allocating power among assets to enable reliable participation in regulation markets, with flexibility envelope definition and state of charge drift correction.
AI.motivation: Hybrid Energy Systems integrating generation sources, storage, and loads can provide grid flexibility, but quantifying maximum flexibility is challenging due to renewable uncertainty and complex real-time power allocation across multiple assets.
AI.method: Rule-based framework for characterizing HES flexibility and systematically allocating power among constituent assets, defining a flexibility envelope as dynamic power boundary, supporting both symmetric and asymmetric flexibility cases, with state of charge drift correction control for battery operation.
AI.result: The framework enables reliable and predictable HES participation in regulation markets, with power-allocation rule benchmarked against optimal dispatch for performance reference, and ensures sustained battery operation and system reliability through drift correction.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a rigorous and practical framework for integrating HES into capacity markets through effective flexibility characterization, addressing challenges of renewable uncertainty and complex power allocation in real-time grid operations.

title: A Distributed SOS Program For Local Stability Analysis of Polynomial PDEs in the PIE Representation
summary: It has recently been shown that the evolution of a state, described by a Partial Differential Equation (PDE), can be more conveniently represented as the evolution of the state's highest spatial derivative (the ``fundamental state''), which lies in $L_2$ and has no boundary conditions (BCs) or continuity constraints. For linear PDEs, this yields a Partial Integral Equation (PIE) parametrized by Partial Integral (PI) operators mapping the fundamental state to the PDE state. In this paper, we show that for polynomial PDEs, the dynamics of the fundamental state can instead be compactly expressed as a distributed polynomial in the fundamental state, parametrized by a new tensor algebra of PI operators acting on the tensor product of the fundamental state. We further define a SOS parametrization of the distributed polynomial and use this to construct a distributed SOS program, for testing local stability of polynomial PDEs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a tensor algebra of Partial Integral (PI) operators to represent polynomial PDEs as distributed polynomials in the fundamental state, enabling distributed SOS programming for stability analysis.
AI.motivation: To develop a more compact and computationally tractable representation for polynomial PDEs by leveraging the fundamental state framework, enabling systematic stability analysis through distributed SOS programming.
AI.method: Extends the fundamental state approach to polynomial PDEs by representing dynamics as distributed polynomials parametrized by PI operators acting on tensor products of the fundamental state, then defines a distributed SOS parametrization for constructing stability analysis programs.
AI.result: Develops a tensor algebra of PI operators for compact representation of polynomial PDE dynamics and constructs a distributed SOS program framework for testing local stability of polynomial PDE systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tensor algebra and distributed SOS framework provides a systematic approach for stability analysis of polynomial PDEs using the fundamental state representation, extending computational tools from finite-dimensional polynomial systems to infinite-dimensional PDE settings.

title: Schrodinger Bridges and Density Steering Problems for Gaussian Mixtures Models in Discrete-Time
summary: In this work, we revisit the discrete-time Schrödinger Bridge (SB) and Density Steering (DS) problems for Gaussian mixture model (GMM) boundary distributions. Building on the existing literature, we construct a set of feasible Markovian policies that transport the initial distribution to the final distribution, and are expressed as mixtures of elementary component-to-component optimal policies. We then study the policy optimization within this feasible set in the context of discrete-time SBs and density-steering problems, respectively. We show that for minimum-effort density-steering problems, the proposed policy achieves the same control cost as existing approaches in the literature. For discrete-time SB problems, the proposed policy yields a cost smaller than or equal to that in the literature, resulting in a less conservative approximation. Finally, we study the continuous-time limit of our proposed discrete-time approach and show that it agrees with recently proposed approximations to the continuous-time SB for GMM boundary distributions. We illustrate this new result through two numerical examples.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new approach for discrete-time Schrödinger Bridge and Density Steering problems with Gaussian mixture model boundary distributions, using mixture policies that improve upon existing approximations.
AI.motivation: To develop less conservative approximations for discrete-time Schrödinger Bridge and Density Steering problems when dealing with Gaussian mixture model boundary distributions, improving upon existing approaches in the literature.
AI.method: Constructs feasible Markovian policies as mixtures of elementary component-to-component optimal policies, then optimizes within this feasible set for both SB and DS problems. Studies the continuous-time limit of the discrete-time approach.
AI.result: For minimum-effort density-steering, achieves same control cost as existing approaches. For discrete-time SB, yields equal or smaller cost than literature, providing less conservative approximation. Continuous-time limit agrees with recently proposed approximations for continuous-time SB with GMM boundary distributions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mixture policy approach provides improved, less conservative solutions for discrete-time Schrödinger Bridge and Density Steering problems with Gaussian mixture models, with theoretical connections to continuous-time approximations.

title: Data-based Low-conservative Nonlinear Safe Control Learning
summary: This paper develops a data-driven safe control framework for nonlinear discrete-time systems with parametric uncertainty and additive disturbances. The proposed approach constructs a data-consistent closed-loop representation that enables controller synthesis and safety certification directly from data. Unlike existing methods that treat unmodeled nonlinearities as global worst-case uncertainties using Lipschitz bounds, the proposed approach embeds nonlinear terms directly into the invariance conditions via a geometry-aware difference-of-convex formulation. This enables facet- and direction-specific convexification, avoiding both nonlinearity cancellation and the excessive conservatism induced by uniform global bounds. We further propose a vertex-dependent controller construction that enforces convexity and contractivity conditions locally on the active facets associated with each vertex, thereby enlarging the class of certifiable invariant sets. For systems subject to additive disturbances, disturbance effects are embedded directly into the verification conditions through optimized, geometry-dependent bounds, rather than via uniform margin inflation, yielding less conservative robust safety guarantees. As a result, the proposed methods can certify substantially larger safe sets, naturally accommodate joint state and input constraints, and provide data-driven safety guarantees. The simulation results show a significant improvement in both nonlinearity tolerance and the size of the certified safe set.

AI.tldr: Data-driven safe control for nonlinear discrete-time systems using geometry-aware convexification and vertex-dependent controller design to reduce conservatism in safety certification.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for safe control of nonlinear systems with uncertainty use global worst-case bounds (Lipschitz) that lead to excessive conservatism, limiting the size of certifiable safe sets and requiring nonlinearity cancellation.
AI.method: Constructs data-consistent closed-loop representation for controller synthesis from data. Uses geometry-aware difference-of-convex formulation to embed nonlinear terms directly into invariance conditions, enabling facet- and direction-specific convexification. Proposes vertex-dependent controller construction that enforces convexity and contractivity locally on active facets. For disturbances, embeds effects directly into verification conditions via optimized geometry-dependent bounds rather than uniform margin inflation.
AI.result: Significantly larger certifiable safe sets compared to existing methods, natural accommodation of joint state and input constraints, data-driven safety guarantees, and improved nonlinearity tolerance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework reduces conservatism in safety certification for nonlinear systems by leveraging geometry-aware convexification and local controller design, enabling larger safe sets and better handling of nonlinearities and disturbances.

title: Safe learning-based control via function-based uncertainty quantification
summary: Uncertainty quantification is essential when deploying learning-based control methods in safety-critical systems. This is commonly realized by constructing uncertainty tubes that enclose the unknown function of interest, e.g., the reward and constraint functions or the underlying dynamics model, with high probability. However, existing approaches for uncertainty quantification typically rely on restrictive assumptions on the unknown function, such as known bounds on functional norms or Lipschitz constants, and struggle with discontinuities. In this paper, we model the unknown function as a random function from which independent and identically distributed realizations can be generated, and construct uncertainty tubes via the scenario approach that hold with high probability and rely solely on the sampled realizations. We integrate these uncertainty tubes into a safe Bayesian optimization algorithm, which we then use to safely tune control parameters on a real Furuta pendulum.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scenario-based approach for constructing uncertainty tubes without restrictive assumptions, and integrates them into safe Bayesian optimization for real-world control tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty quantification methods for learning-based control rely on restrictive assumptions (known functional norm bounds, Lipschitz constants) and struggle with discontinuities, limiting their practical applicability in safety-critical systems.
AI.method: Model the unknown function as a random function with i.i.d. realizations, construct uncertainty tubes via the scenario approach using only sampled realizations, and integrate these tubes into a safe Bayesian optimization framework.
AI.result: The approach successfully tunes control parameters on a real Furuta pendulum, demonstrating practical applicability without requiring restrictive assumptions about the unknown function.
AI.conclusion: The scenario-based uncertainty quantification method provides a practical alternative to assumption-heavy approaches and enables safe learning-based control in real-world safety-critical systems.

title: Learning Neural Network Controllers with Certified Robust Performance via Adversarial Training
summary: Neural network (NN) controllers achieve strong empirical performance on nonlinear dynamical systems, yet deploying them in safety-critical settings requires robustness to disturbances and uncertainty. We present a method for jointly synthesizing NN controllers and dissipativity certificates that formally guarantee robust closed-loop performance using adversarial training, in which we use counterexamples to the robust dissipativity condition to guide training. Verification is done post-training using alpha,beta-CROWN, a branch-and-bound-based method that enables direct analysis of the nonlinear dynamical system. The proposed method uses quadratic constraints (QCs) only for characterization of non-parametric uncertainties. The method is tested in numerical experiments on maximizing the volume of the set on which a system is certified to be robustly dissipative. Our method certifies regions up to 78 times larger than the region certified by a linear matrix inequality-based approach that we derive for comparison.

AI.tldr: A method for jointly training neural network controllers and dissipativity certificates using adversarial training to guarantee robust closed-loop performance, with verification via alpha,beta-CROWN.
AI.motivation: Neural network controllers show strong empirical performance on nonlinear dynamical systems, but safety-critical applications require formal robustness guarantees against disturbances and uncertainty.
AI.method: Joint synthesis of NN controllers and dissipativity certificates using adversarial training, where counterexamples to robust dissipativity guide training. Verification is performed post-training using alpha,beta-CROWN (branch-and-bound method) for direct analysis of nonlinear dynamics. Quadratic constraints are used only for characterizing non-parametric uncertainties.
AI.result: The method certifies regions up to 78 times larger than those certified by a linear matrix inequality-based approach derived for comparison, demonstrating superior certification volume.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables formal robustness guarantees for NN controllers in safety-critical applications through joint controller-certificate synthesis and adversarial training, with verification using modern branch-and-bound methods.

title: Polynomial Constraints for Robustness Analysis of Nonlinear Systems
summary: This paper presents a framework for abstracting uncertain or non-polynomial components of dynamical systems using polynomial constraints. This enables the application of polynomial-based analysis tools, such as sum-of-squares programming, to a broader class of non-polynomial systems. A numerical method for constructing these constraints is proposed. The relationship between polynomial constraints and existing integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) is investigated, providing transformations of IQCs into polynomial constraints. The effectiveness of polynomial constraints in characterizing nonlinearities is validated via numerical examples to compute inner estimates of the region of attraction for two systems.

AI.tldr: Framework for abstracting uncertain/non-polynomial dynamical system components using polynomial constraints to enable polynomial-based analysis tools like SOS programming for broader system classes.
AI.motivation: Enable application of polynomial-based analysis tools (e.g., sum-of-squares programming) to broader classes of non-polynomial dynamical systems by abstracting uncertain or non-polynomial components.
AI.method: Proposes framework for abstracting uncertain/non-polynomial components using polynomial constraints, numerical method for constructing constraints, and investigates relationship with integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) including transformations from IQCs to polynomial constraints.
AI.result: Validates effectiveness of polynomial constraints in characterizing nonlinearities via numerical examples computing inner estimates of region of attraction for two systems.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial constraints provide effective abstraction method for non-polynomial system components, enabling application of polynomial-based analysis tools to broader system classes, with demonstrated utility in region of attraction estimation.

title: Making Every Bit Count for $A$-Optimal State Estimation
summary: We study the problem of controlling how a limited communication bandwidth budget is allocated across heterogeneously quantized sensor measurements. The performance criterion is the trace of the error covariance matrix of the linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) state estimator, i.e., an $A$-optimal design criterion. Minimizing this criterion with a bit budget constraint yields a nonconvex optimization problem. We derive a formula that reduces each evaluation of the gradient to a single Cholesky factorization. This enables efficient optimization by both a projection-free Frank-Wolfe method (with a computable convergence certificate) and an interior point method with L-BFGS Hessian approximation over the problem's continuous relaxation. A largest remainder rounding procedure recovers integer bit allocations with a bound on the quality of the rounded solution. Numerical experiments in IEEE power grid test cases with up to 300 buses compare both solvers and demonstrate that the analytic gradient is the key computational enabler for both methods. Additionally, the heterogeneous bit allocation is compared to standard uniform bit allocation on the 500 bus IEEE power grid test case.

AI.tldr: Efficient optimization of heterogeneous bit allocation for sensor quantization in state estimation using analytic gradient computation and two optimization methods.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the problem of optimally allocating limited communication bandwidth across heterogeneously quantized sensor measurements for state estimation, where minimizing the trace of the error covariance matrix (A-optimal design) with bit budget constraints leads to a nonconvex optimization problem.
AI.method: Derived an analytic gradient formula that reduces each gradient evaluation to a single Cholesky factorization. Used two optimization approaches: 1) projection-free Frank-Wolfe method with computable convergence certificate, and 2) interior point method with L-BFGS Hessian approximation over the continuous relaxation. Applied largest remainder rounding to recover integer bit allocations with quality bounds.
AI.result: The analytic gradient enables efficient optimization for both methods. Numerical experiments on IEEE power grid test cases (up to 300 buses) compare both solvers and demonstrate the gradient's computational importance. Heterogeneous bit allocation outperforms standard uniform allocation on the 500-bus test case.
AI.conclusion: The derived analytic gradient is the key computational enabler for solving the nonconvex heterogeneous bit allocation problem. Both optimization methods (Frank-Wolfe and interior point) benefit from this gradient, enabling efficient solutions that outperform uniform bit allocation in power grid state estimation applications.
